items.title: Why an imported earned value of 9999 is thrown away
items.body:
The import code does not trust the stored XP number. For each ticket it reads `data.passedTests[t.id]` and throws "Invalid passed tests." if any name is not a string or is not in that ticket's `testNames`. It keeps the unique names (`new Set`) and then sets `result.earned[t.id] = testXP(t, names.length, p.hintsUsed)`. So the 9999 in the file is never read for the result; XP is recalculated from the one valid passed test name. DECISIONS.md: "reward totals are recalculated from known test names".

Why the others are wrong:
- Size limits are one check among several, and the stored earned value is not kept.
- There is no "cap at xp" step; the value is replaced by a fresh `testXP` result.
- A large earned value is not a reason to reject; the code only rejects bad test names (and bad shapes).

excerpts.quote: const names = data.passedTests[t.id] ?? []; if ( !Array.isArray(names) || names.some((n) => typeof n !== "string" || !t.testNames?.includes(n)) ) throw new Error("Invalid passed tests."); result.passedTests[t.id] = [...new Set(names)]; result.earned[t.id] = testXP( t, result.passedTests[t.id].length, p.hintsUsed, );
reward totals are recalculated from known test names

items.title: Why a busy loop and a stuck promise time out differently
items.body:
There are two different clocks. Inside the sandbox, `harness.ts` sets `deadline = start + 2500` and `guard()` throws "Execution timed out. Check loops and recursive calls…" once the time is past it. The compiler inserts calls to `guard()` into loops and function bodies, so `while (true) {}` keeps calling it and fails after about 2.5 s with that message.

`await new Promise(() => {})` is different: the promise never settles, so no code runs at all and `guard()` is never called. Only the host notices, through its own 3000 ms `setTimeout` in `client.ts`, with the message "Execution timed out after 3 seconds…". README exercise 2 states this exact contrast.

Why the others are wrong:
- Compilation (30 s) only transpiles; it does not detect loops.
- The guard does not reject promises; a promise that never settles runs no guarded code. The 10 s limit is for sandbox start-up.
- Only the promise waits for the 3 s deadline; the loop is stopped first by the 2.5 s guard.

excerpts.quote: const deadline = start + 2500; const guard = () => { if (performance.now() > deadline) throw new Error( "Execution timed out. Check loops and recursive calls; each run has a 3-second budget.", );
timeout = setTimeout( () => finish( failure( "Execution timed out after 3 seconds. Check for an infinite loop, unresolved promise, or runaway recursion. Your code has been saved.", ), ), 3000,

2. **Goal:** distinguish the 2.5 s guard from the 3 s deadline. **Check:** a `while (true) {}` loop fails with the harness message "Execution timed out. Check loops and recursive calls…", while `await new Promise(() => {})` fails with the host's "Execution timed out after 3 seconds…" message.

items.title: Why the second skipped day resets the streak to 1
items.body:
In `updateStreak`, `gap` is the number of days since your last passing day. A gap of 1 means "the next day". A gap of 2 means you skipped exactly one day. The new streak is `streak + 1` only when `gap === 1 || (gap === 2 && !freezeUsed)`; otherwise it is `1`. The first skip uses the grace day, and the next line sets `freezeUsed: freezeUsed || gap === 2`, so it becomes true. Nothing in this function ever sets it back to false. On the second skip gap is 2 again but `freezeUsed` is true, so the streak becomes 1. The README says the same: one missed day can be bridged once and the freeze is not refilled.

Why the others are wrong:
- No code counts seven passing days or refills the grace day.
- The result is 1, never 0, and passing twice is not a rule.
- A gap of 2 is bridged only while `!freezeUsed`, not always.

excerpts.quote: if (lastDay === day) return { lastDay, streak, freezeUsed }; const gap = lastDay ? dayNumber(day) - dayNumber(lastDay) : Infinity; return { lastDay: day, streak: gap === 1 || (gap === 2 && !freezeUsed) ? streak + 1 : 1, freezeUsed: freezeUsed || gap === 2, };
- Streaks use local calendar days and advance on a day with a passing test. One missed day can be bridged once. The freeze is not automatically refilled.

items.title: Why two results named A do not pass a two-test suite
items.body:
`suitePassed` returns true only if every condition joined by `&&` holds. Two results named A pass most of them: there is no error, the count is 2 and equals `known.size`, and every result passed and has a known name. The last line is what fails: `new Set(result.results.map((t) => t.name)).size === known.size`. A Set drops repeats, so the names {A, A} become {A}, size 1, and 1 is not 2. This line makes sure the results cover each distinct test, so one test cannot be counted twice.

Why the others are wrong:
- "It returns true" ignores that last distinct-names line.
- Nothing in the function lowercases names, and it does not label anything "forged"; it just compares sizes.
- `result.error` comes from the run itself. Repeated names do not set it; the check is on line 26 and is separate.

excerpts.quote: export function suitePassed(ticket: Ticket, result: RunResult) { const known = new Set(ticket.testNames ?? []); return ( !ticket.comingSoon && known.size > 0 && !result.error && result.results.length === known.size && result.results.every((t) => t.passed && known.has(t.name)) && new Set(result.results.map((t) => t.name)).size === known.size ); }

items.title: Start here: how Ship It runs, checks and rewards your code
items.body:
Ship It is a browser coding trainer. You get a ticket, write code in an editor, and hidden tests run in a locked-down sandbox. Your progress lives only in your own browser.

Read in this order:

1. **README.md**, sections "Architecture", "Sandbox and test execution" and "Learning and rewards". The diagram shows the path: editor, compiler worker, sandbox iframe, then a worker or a DOM document, then results.
2. **README.md "Reading the code"**. Every claim above it has a file and line anchor. Open those anchors; most quizzes in this pack are about the code they point at.
3. **DECISIONS.md**. One bullet per design choice, with the reason. Read it slowly: the quizzes often ask *why*, not *what*.
4. **content/README.md**. How an author writes a ticket, its tests and its `testNames`, and how `npm run validate-content` checks a ticket before it ships.
5. **LEARNING_REVIEW.md**. What the app can and cannot measure about learning.

The main code files are `src/runner/` (sandbox), `src/store.ts` (all saved state) and `src/learning.ts` (recall and pass rules). When a quiz names a function, open it and read it line by line before you answer.

excerpts.quote: A project-first coding trainer focused on moving from junior foundations toward independent feature ownership and senior engineering judgment. Predict a failure, write code, verify behavior, explain a decision, then revisit from memory.
Anchors for the claims above, so they can be checked rather than trusted:

readMore.why: Each design choice with its reason, the source of most why-questions.
How tickets, hidden tests and testNames are authored and validated.

items.title: Why the sandbox needs a CSP on top of the fetch stubs
items.body:
`worker-runtime.ts` replaces a fixed list of names (fetch, XMLHttpRequest, WebSocket, EventSource, importScripts, Worker, SharedWorker) with functions that throw. That only covers the names on the list. Code can make requests in other ways, such as a dynamic `import()` of a remote URL or a resource like an image. DECISIONS.md names these: "Remote dynamic imports, resource elements, and alternative network APIs". The CSP is enforced by the browser for every request, whatever API starts it, so `connect-src 'none'` and the other rules close the paths the list missed. The `client.ts` comment lists what the policy blocks: "Dynamic imports, requests, images, forms, and external scripts".

Why the others are wrong:
- The CSP is about network and resources, not about the host's cookies.
- The stubs are defined with `writable: false, configurable: false`, so they cannot be deleted.
- The stubs are installed when the worker runtime loads, before learner code runs.

excerpts.quote: for (const name of [ "fetch", "XMLHttpRequest", "WebSocket", "EventSource", "importScripts", "Worker", "SharedWorker", ]) { Object.defineProperty(globalThis, name, { value: () => { throw new Error( "Network and nested workers are disabled in this sandbox. Use the injected API mock.", ); }, writable: false, configurable: false, }); }
// A blob worker inherits this opaque-origin frame's CSP. Dynamic imports, // requests, images, forms, and external scripts are blocked by the browser.

items.title: Why rerunning passing code adds no XP
items.body:
`recordRun` does not add points per run. It rebuilds the list of passed test names: the old names plus the names that passed now, put through `new Set` so repeats vanish. Then it computes `earned = testXP(ticket, names.length, ...)` and the change `delta = earned - (s.earned[id] ?? 0)`. If a rerun passes the same tests, the set of names is the same size, `earned` is the same number, and `delta` is 0. XP grows only when a new test name passes for the first time. The README: "Each unique passing test earns its share of the ticket's XP. Reruns cannot farm points."

Why the others are wrong:
- There is no daily cap in this code; there is simply nothing new to add.
- Reruns are allowed and are recorded; the recompute is what keeps XP flat.
- The calculation is not skipped for passed tickets; it runs and gives a delta of zero.

excerpts.quote: const names = [ ...new Set([ ...(s.passedTests[id] ?? []), ...result.results .filter((t) => t.passed && known.has(t.name)) .map((t) => t.name), ]), ]; const earned = testXP(ticket, names.length, old.hintsUsed), delta = earned - (s.earned[id] ?? 0);
- Each unique passing test earns its share of the ticket’s XP. Reruns cannot farm points. Passed test names are retained as milestones even if a later draft regresses.

items.title: Why a double-quoted test name fails validate-content
items.body:
`seed()` builds `testNames` with the regex `/test\('([^']+)'/g`. It only matches `test('` followed by a single quote. `test("Handles empty input", ...)` uses double quotes, so the regex skips it and the name is missing from `testNames`. The test itself still runs in the harness and appears in the results. `validate-content` then fails the ticket when `result.results.length !== ticket.testNames?.length`: the run has one more result than the declared names. README "Reading the code" describes exactly this case.

Why the others are wrong:
- The harness registers tests by calling `test(...)`; it does not care about quote style, so nothing is refused.
- The regex only allows a single quote, so the double-quoted name is not matched.
- Double quotes are valid JavaScript, so there is no syntax error.

excerpts.quote: testNames: [...s.tests.matchAll(/test\('([^']+)'/g)].map((m) => m[1]),
if ( result.error || !result.results.length || result.results.some((t) => !t.passed) || result.results.length !== ticket.testNames?.length ) {

- **Test names.** `seed()` extracts names with `/test\('([^']+)'/g` (`curriculum.ts:49`), so only single-quoted test names are recognized. A double-quoted test would run but be missing from `testNames`; `scripts/validate-content.ts:17-22` catches that as a count mismatch.

items.title: Why the worker is created inside the sandbox iframe
items.body:
A worker made from a blob URL takes its security policy from the document that creates it. The sandbox iframe has a strict CSP written into its `srcdoc`: `connect-src 'none'`, `img-src 'none'`, `default-src 'none'` and more. The comment in `client.ts` says it directly: "A blob worker inherits this opaque-origin frame's CSP." That is why the host sends bridge code into the iframe and the iframe creates the worker. If the host page created the worker, it would get the host page's looser policy, and the browser would no longer block network requests and other resources for learner code. DECISIONS.md: "Worker runtimes are created inside the restricted iframe so blob workers inherit its policy."

Why the others are wrong:
- Sibling modules are compiled into the project the worker receives; who creates the worker does not change that.
- Workers never have DOM access, whoever creates them.
- The iframe is a security boundary (its CSP and sandbox flags), not only a way to stop runs.

excerpts.quote: // A blob worker inherits this opaque-origin frame's CSP. Dynamic imports, // requests, images, forms, and external scripts are blocked by the browser.
Worker runtimes are created inside the restricted iframe so blob workers inherit its policy.

items.title: Why hints stopped costing XP
items.body:
`hintMultiplier` always returns 1, so `testXP` gives the same XP with or without hints. The reason is a learning argument, written in DECISIONS.md and LEARNING_REVIEW.md. The review found that "Hint penalties, speed, and fewer lines could reward counterproductive shortcuts": a penalty pushes you to stay stuck instead of asking for help. The README says asking for help is compatible with learning, and later recall (done without help) is where independent practice is checked. That is the reasoning in the key.

Why the others are wrong:
- None of the docs talk about how often hints were used.
- Recomputing old backups is a consequence of the policy ("Existing backups are recalculated"), not the reason for it.
- Hints are still recorded: the README says "Hints are recorded but never reduce XP", and `hintsUsed` is kept.

excerpts.quote: export function hintMultiplier(_hints: number) { return 1; }

- Hints are recorded but never reduce XP. Existing backups are recalculated under this policy. Asking for help is compatible with learning; later recall gives a separate opportunity to practice independently.
Hint penalties, speed, and fewer lines could reward counterproductive shortcuts

items.title: Why a recall started early does not advance the schedule
items.body:
When a recall session passes, `recordRun` computes `spaced`. It is true only if the suite passed, the recall was not already passed, it was not assisted, there is a due time, and `Date.parse(recall.startedAt) >= due`. The schedule counter is `recalls: record.recalls + (spaced ? 1 : 0)`. If you started one day before it was due, `startedAt` is before `due`, so `spaced` is false and `recalls` stays the same. The pass still counts as practice; it just does not move the schedule. LEARNING_REVIEW.md: "Early practice is allowed but does not advance the schedule."

Why the others are wrong:
- There is no "shorter interval" path; the counter simply does not change.
- Early sessions can run and pass; the code does not block them.
- Early is a different condition from assisted, and nothing removes existing recalls; the count is only ever increased by 0 or 1.

excerpts.quote: const spaced = passed && !recall.passed && !recall.assisted && due !== undefined && Date.parse(recall.startedAt) >= due; const nextRecord = { ...record, recalls: record.recalls + (spaced ? 1 : 0),
Early practice is allowed but does not advance the schedule.

items.title: Why a hint during recall blocks the advance but costs nothing
items.body:
`useHint` checks first whether the ticket has an active recall. If so, it returns early and only changes the recall record to `assisted: true`. Because it returns before the normal hint code, `hintsUsed` is not touched. Later, when the suite passes, `recordRun` counts the session as "spaced" (and advances the schedule) only if `!recall.assisted` and a few other conditions hold. So an assisted session can pass but cannot move the recall forward. DECISIONS.md says assisted sessions "cannot advance" the schedule.

Why the others are wrong:
- The recall does not advance at all, so no interval is reset to 1 day.
- `hintsUsed` does not rise in this branch, and hints never cost XP anyway.
- Hints are not disabled during recall; using one is recorded as `assisted`.

excerpts.quote: useHint: (id) => set((s) => { const record = s.learning[id]; if (record?.recall?.active) return { learning: { ...s.learning, [id]: { ...record, recall: { ...record.recall, assisted: true }, }, }, };
const spaced = passed && !recall.passed && !recall.assisted && due !== undefined && Date.parse(recall.startedAt) >= due;

items.title: Concept: the layers of the sandbox and their time limits
items.body:
Learner code never runs on the main app page. It passes through layers, and each layer has one job.

- A **compiler worker** turns your files and tests into plain JavaScript. While it does that it adds small time checks into loops and function bodies.
- The host page creates a **sandbox iframe**: a separate document with its own strict Content Security Policy (CSP). A CSP is a rule list the browser itself enforces, such as "no network connections".
- Inside that iframe, pure-JS tickets run in a **Web Worker** (a background thread with no DOM). DOM and React tickets run in the iframe's own document.
- A **message bridge** sends the results back to the host, which only accepts messages from that frame.

There is not one timer but several, owned by different layers. The README lists them in one line. When a quiz describes code that hangs, first ask: which layer notices, and whose timer fires first? Then find that timer in the code.

excerpts.quote: A compiler Web Worker transpiles learner files and tests to CommonJS. It reports syntax errors and injects time guards into synchronous loops and function bodies.
Browser DOM and React tickets execute in the iframe’s own document with locally bundled React 18 and Testing Library.

- **Four separate time limits.** Compilation 30 s (`src/runner/client.ts:38-44`), sandbox start-up 10 s (`client.ts:108-116`), execution 3 s from the frame's `ready` message (`client.ts:79-87`), and an in-sandbox guard that throws after 2.5 s inside instrumented loops and functions (`src/runner/harness.ts:111-116`).

readMore.why: The host side: creates the iframe, writes its CSP and runs the timers.
The in-sandbox test harness and its guard function.

items.title: Concept: where progress, XP and recall state are kept
items.body:
All saved learning state lives in one Zustand store in `src/store.ts`, persisted to the browser's localStorage. Pass rules and the recall schedule are helpers in `src/learning.ts`.

Useful words:

- **testNames**: the list of hidden test names a ticket declares. Many rules compare run results against this list.
- **passedTests**: for each ticket, the test names you have passed so far.
- **earned**: the XP stored for each ticket.
- **hintsUsed**: how many hints you opened.
- **recall**: a separate practice session on a ticket you already passed, on a 1/3/7/21-day schedule.

A good habit for this pack: when a quiz asks "what happens to XP or recall", find the function that writes that field (`recordRun`, `useHint`, the import code, `updateStreak`) and trace the exact condition. The README and DECISIONS describe the intent in words; the store code is what decides.

excerpts.quote: export const recallIntervals = [1, 3, 7, 21];

- **Progress rules.** Storage key `ship-it.progress.v1` (`src/store.ts:12`); streak with one lifetime grace day (`store.ts:66-79`); recall intervals `[1, 3, 7, 21]` days (`src/learning.ts:10-17`); imported results are rejected if any name is not one of the ticket's `testNames` (`store.ts:337`).

readMore.why: The whole persistent state, including recordRun, useHint, imports and streaks.
Why recall exists and what it does not prove.
